memories.memory_text: I remember the cold air and seeing mourners arrive for the funeral service at the Second Funeral Parlor while I stood there, cut off and watching from the outside.

memories.memory_text: I remember Mickey walking into my office, yelling at me about being unprepared for the case, knocking my drink out of my hand, slapping me, and telling me he's done helping me because I've betrayed the trust of the clients and wasted his effort.

memories.memory_text: I heard Mickey tell me he was done helping me, saying life is too short and he's too old to keep enabling me, and that this was the end of his support.

memories.memory_text: After Mickey left, I sat on the sofa and reached for a cigarette from the side table, my hand shaking as I took it.

memories.memory_text: I listened to Sally tell me how her sister doesn't know who's visiting, how her husband left her with the kids, how the care home wants fifty thousand dollars, and how Father Laughlin said it was God's will—she was carrying all of it and just needed someone to hear her.

memories.memory_text: I met with Sally and Dick Doneghy in my office to discuss their sister's medical malpractice case, where I committed to giving them a chance in court despite the financial and emotional burdens they're facing.

grounded_facts: Dick asks about the financial implications of hiring Galvin, showing concern for practical consequences.
memories.memory_text: I was asked what this was going to cost, so I knew Dick was worried about the financial side of hiring me.

memories.memory_text: I explained that I'd take the case on a contingency, keeping one-third of any settlement, so they wouldn't have to pay anything upfront.

memories.memory_text: I was told that Dr. David Gruber, a prominent surgeon, wants to meet with me tonight at seven at the hospital to talk about testifying in the Deborah Ann Kaye case.

memories.memory_text: I called out to Dr. Gruber and walked over to him at his locker to start the conversation.

Dr. Gruber confirms Galvin's identity and agrees to speak, but insists on walking while talking due to time pressure.
memories.memory_text: I saw Dr. Gruber turn and acknowledge me, confirming he knew who I was, and I noticed he agreed to talk only if we walked while speaking because he was in a rush.

Gruber tells Galvin that he has read the hospital report on Deborah Ann Kaye, signaling his involvement and awareness.
memories.memory_text: I remember Gruber telling me, 'I read the hospital report on your client,' which made it clear he had been looking into Deborah Ann Kaye's case.

grounded_facts: Gruber and Galvin walk together through a hospital corridor at night, discussing the case of Deborah Ann Kaye.
memories.memory_text: I was walking with Gruber through a hospital corridor at night, hurrying toward an exit, as we talked about Deborah Ann Kaye's case.

memories.memory_text: I told Gruber that the Archdiocese called and wants to settle the case, and I explained that I'm considering it in the interests of the family because you can never predict what a jury might do, especially with St. Catherine's being such a respected institution.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Gruber that the doctors, Marx and Towler, murdered the patient by giving her the wrong anesthetic, which killed her and her child.

grounded_facts: Gruber questions Galvin's decision to settle, expressing disbelief and moral outrage, implying Galvin is abandoning justice.

memories.memory_text: I brought up meeting again to get a deposition, telling Gruber it was in the interests of the family, and we agreed to meet next Tuesday night at the same place.

memories.memory_text: I remember meeting Gruber in the hospital parking lot at night, where we talked about the case while he was getting into his car.

grounded_facts: Gruber and Galvin schedule a meeting for Tuesday at seven o'clock to review Gruber's testimony.
memories.memory_text: I learned from Gruber that he can meet on Tuesday at seven o'clock to go over his testimony, and I wrote that down in my appointment book.

grounded_facts: Galvin asks Gruber why he is helping, seeking to understand his motivation.
memories.memory_text: I asked Gruber why he was helping, wanting to understand what was really driving him.

memories.memory_text: I was told by Gruber that he wanted to do right, and he asked if that wasn't why I was doing it too.

memories.memory_text: I offered the young woman a drink to start a conversation, hoping to connect with her.

memories.memory_text: I remember the quiet bar that night, how I tried talking to her, and how the bartender kept my drink coming while I sat alone after she left.

memories.memory_text: After she left, I said to myself, 'It's a long road that has no turning,' because I felt how alone I am on this path.

grounded_facts: Galvin focuses on a legal pad with proposed settlement figures, ultimately circling $225,000.00 multiple times, indicating a decision or strong preference.
memories.memory_text: I focused on the legal pad, crossing out $150,000 and $250,000, and I kept circling $225,000.00 because that felt right.

Galvin reassures the caller that their actions come from love and that they must continue living their own life.
memories.memory_text: I spoke softly on the phone, offering comfort and reassurance—I told the caller they were just following their life, that they had to move out West, that it doesn't help to stay, and I reminded them that I know they love her, that they're acting out of love, before I said, 'Well, bless you, too. Good night,' and hung up.

grounded_facts: Galvin is alone in his apartment at night, engaged in phone conversation, legal planning, and personal mourning.
memories.memory_text: I was alone in my apartment at night, sitting in the armchair with my beer and cigarettes on the table, a legal pad in my lap, remembering her as I looked at the photo of the blonde woman in the silver frame—the same one from the news clip, laughing on a sailboat, with my wedding ring resting beside her in the pile of change.

grounded_facts: After hanging up, Galvin looks at a photo of a blonde woman (implied to be his late wife), sighs deeply, and turns off the light, entering a moment of solitude and grief.
memories.memory_text: After I hung up the phone, I looked at the photo of my late wife in the silver frame, sighed deeply, and turned off the lamp, sitting alone in the dark with my grief.

grounded_facts: Galvin sits in the darkened ward of Deborah Ann Kaye, reviewing her file and photo, before being interrupted by nursing staff.
memories.memory_text: I sat in the darkened ward with Deborah Ann Kaye's file on my lap, looking at her photo and the notes I'd written, trying to make sense of what happened to her.

grounded_facts: The nurse confronts Galvin for being in a restricted area, challenging his right to be there.
memories.memory_text: I remember the nurse confronting me, saying I wasn't allowed to be in that area and telling me I couldn't stay there.

grounded_facts: In response to the nurse's challenge, Galvin states he is Deborah Ann Kaye's attorney, positioning himself as having legitimate access.
Galvin, after being confronted by a nurse, states that he is Deborah Ann Kaye's attorney, asserting his presence in the restricted ward.
memories.memory_text: When the nurse challenged me, I told her I was Deborah Ann Kaye's attorney, hoping that would justify why I was there.

memories.memory_text: I was in a formal meeting with Bishop Brophy and a young priest, where they presented me with a settlement offer from St. Catherine's Hospital about Deborah Ann Kaye's case, and I could feel the weight of what they were really asking.

grounded_facts: Galvin confronts the Bishop, accusing him and the hospital of accepting a payoff to conceal the truth about Deborah Ann Kaye's condition and the malpractice committed by the doctors.
memories.memory_text: I confronted the Bishop, telling him that no one would know the truth—that Deborah Ann Kaye trusted those doctors with her life and now she's in a coma, with no one to speak for her but me.

grounded_facts: Galvin decides not to accept the $210,000 settlement offer from St. Catherine's Hospital, recognizing that taking the money would compromise his integrity and reduce him to a corrupt ambulance chaser.
memories.memory_text: I admitted to myself and the young priest that I came to take their money, but I realized I can't accept it—because if I do, I'm just a rich ambulance chaser, and I'd lose whatever integrity I have left.

grounded_facts: The Young Priest challenges Galvin’s decision by probing the state of his law practice, implying that his refusal of money is impractical given his financial desperation.
memories.memory_text: I remember the young priest questioning me about my law practice, asking how it was doing, and I told him it wasn't too good—I only had one client.

grounded_facts: A group of ambulance chasers, including Mickey Morrissey, are gathered in the Lawyers Room, waiting for clients while engaging in casual activities like reading, phone calls, and card games.
memories.memory_text: I walked into the Lawyers Room and saw a bunch of ambulance chasers, including Mickey Morrissey, just waiting around, reading or on the phone, and Mickey was in the corner playing Gin with a friend.

grounded_facts: Galvin asserts urgency and control by interrupting Mickey’s card game and physically pulling him away to talk.
Galvin interrupts Mickey's card game and forcibly takes him out of the Lawyers Room for a private conversation.
memories.memory_text: I interrupted Mickey’s card game, told him I had to talk, and when he asked what I wanted, I said, 'Come on. Let's get a drink,' then led him out of the room to speak privately.

grounded_facts: A heated confrontation between Mickey and Galvin at the courthouse over whether to accept the settlement or proceed with the trial.
memories.memory_text: I remember the heated argument with Mickey at the courthouse, where he kept pressuring me to take the settlement, yelling that I was crazy and that Eddie Concannon would destroy us if we went to trial.

grounded_facts: Mickey tries to convince Galvin to drop the case and take the money, warning of the powerful opposition.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mickey yelling at me, trying to get me to drop the case and take the settlement, saying we should just let them buy it and go hunting in New Hampshire — he kept telling me I already won when they offered the money, and warned me not to mess with the Archdiocese because Eddie Concannon is dangerous, like the 'Prince of Fuckin' Darkness,' and could make up witnesses just to destroy me.

grounded_facts: Galvin resolves to try the case despite the settlement offer, motivated by a sense of moral duty to stand up for the deceased girl.
memories.memory_text: I knew I had to try this case because I needed to stand up for that girl — I told Mickey I have to do it, that it was the right thing, and that I had to help her even though she was gone.

grounded_facts: Galvin repeatedly asks Mickey to support him in trying the case, invoking their shared values.
memories.memory_text: I kept asking Mickey to help me, saying I needed his support, pleading with him to stand by me because I couldn't do it alone and we had to fight for this together.

grounded_facts: Galvin asserts that the hospital's admittance form, which states the patient ate nine hours before admission, is incorrect, countering Mickey's skepticism with the sister's testimony of a recent meal.
memories.memory_text: I told Mickey the admittance form was wrong because the patient's sister said she had eaten recently, even though he shot it down, saying her testimony wouldn't hold up with the jury.

grounded_facts: Galvin emphasizes Dr. Gruber's credibility and likability to convince Mickey of his strategic value in court.
Galvin presents Dr. Gruber as a favorable expert witness who will testify that the patient received the wrong anesthetic due to her heart condition and that she reported stomach pains upon admission.
memories.memory_text: I told Mickey that my Dr. Gruber would testify the patient got the wrong anesthetic because of her heart condition and that she came in complaining of stomach pains, and I emphasized how credible and likable he is by saying the jury's going to love him just like Dr. Kildare.

grounded_facts: Galvin and Mickey review case materials, discuss witness credibility, and plan legal arguments in a law library at night.
memories.memory_text: I was with Mickey late in the law library, going over the case materials—we were both smoking, talking quietly, and I remember rummaging through papers while arguing that the nurses' depositions painted the doctors as infallible, but Mickey just said no to my point.

grounded_facts: Galvin asks Mickey why Mary Rooney, an obstetrical nurse still working at the hospital, has not given a deposition.
memories.memory_text: I asked Mickey why Mary Rooney, an obstetrical nurse still working at the hospital, hasn't given a deposition.

memories.memory_text: I noticed that Mary Rooney, an obstetrical nurse who worked at the hospital, hasn't provided a deposition, and I wondered why she's staying silent and whether she might be a relevant witness.

grounded_facts: Mickey responds to Galvin's comment about getting laid with a witty remark and leaves.
memories.memory_text: I made a comment about getting laid, and Mickey shot back with 'Don't leave your best work in the sheets' before saluting and walking off.

grounded_facts: Galvin decides to go talk to Laura at the bar, initiating a romantic encounter.
memories.memory_text: I decided to go talk to Laura at the bar, so I motioned with my head and then took my drink to move down to her.

grounded_facts: After a tense exchange, Laura reveals her name is Laura and agrees to follow Galvin, marking a shift in their relationship.
memories.memory_text: I saw Laura finally reveal her name and start following me, despite her hesitation, after I told her I changed my life and she mentioned changing her room at the Hotel.

grounded_facts: Galvin uses charm and confidence to engage Laura in conversation and persuade her to join him for dinner.
memories.memory_text: I used my charm and confidence to talk to Laura, asking her about her apartment and hotel, questioning why she called off her wedding, and telling her she was a beautiful woman to win her over and get her to agree to dinner with me.

grounded_facts: A chance encounter between Galvin and Laura at O'Rourke's Pub, reigniting their connection from the previous night.
memories.memory_text: I approached Laura at O'Rourke's Pub and told her I changed my life today, then we bantered back and forth—she questioned if I was a cop, I told her I'm a lawyer, I bet her a hundred dollars she'd join me for dinner, I introduced myself as Frank, and I said she came back to see me, and even when she hesitated, she followed me anyway and I told her she's a beautiful woman.

grounded_facts: Galvin and Laura share a late-night dinner at O'Rourke's, during which they discuss the nature of justice and Galvin's upcoming trial.
memories.memory_text: I had dinner with Laura at O'Rourke's late one night, and we talked about justice while sharing drinks and cigarettes.

grounded_facts: Galvin reveals his inner motivation for taking on the case — the desire to do something right — in response to Laura's questioning.
memories.memory_text: When Laura asked me if I was really going to do something right in this case, I realized she was pushing me to admit my true reason for taking it — and I told her that's what I'm going to try to do.

grounded_facts: Galvin expresses his resolve to try to do something right in the upcoming trial, indicating a personal commitment to seek justice for the weak.
memories.memory_text: I told Laura that I'm going to try to do something right in this trial, because even though people act like justice is a sham, deep down they still hope for it.

grounded_facts: Laura tells Galvin it's all right to leave the photo visible, signaling acceptance or acknowledgment of the emotional weight without stopping the progression toward intimacy.
memories.memory_text: I heard Laura tell me it was all right to leave the photo of my wife visible, and that allowed me to stay present in the moment with her.

grounded_facts: An unplanned, emotionally charged moment of potential intimacy between Galvin and Laura in Galvin's bedroom late at night.
Galvin notices the framed picture of his wife on the bedside table and begins to turn it face down upon realizing Laura's presence, indicating discomfort or guilt about the intimacy unfolding.
memories.memory_text: I was in my bedroom late at night, feeling unsettled with Laura close by, and when I saw the framed picture of my wife on the bedside table, I started to turn it face down because I felt guilty about the intimacy that might happen.

grounded_facts: Galvin looks at the clock, finishes his drink, and departs the courthouse bar.
memories.memory_text: I looked at the clock, finished my drink, and picked up my briefcase before heading out the door.

grounded_facts: Concannon extends his hand and introduces himself, though Galvin notes they've met before.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Concannon extended his hand and said, 'Ed Concannon,' as if we hadn't met before—I immediately told him, 'Frank Galvin. We've met before.'

grounded_facts: Galvin explicitly declines the settlement offer, committing to take the case to trial.
memories.memory_text: I told them we are going to try the case, no matter the pressure to settle.

grounded_facts: Concannon states that the Archdiocese offers $210,000 to settle the case, effective only if accepted before trial begins.
memories.memory_text: I was told the Archdiocese offered $210,000 to settle the case, but it would only count if I accepted before trial started.

grounded_facts: Judge Sweeney implies that Galvin should accept the offer, citing his past disciplinary issues and lack of strong professional standing.
Judge Sweeney questions Galvin's competence and judgment, implying he should take the settlement due to his weak professional history.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Judge Sweeney that I should take the settlement because of my past disciplinary issues and weak professional standing, and he even said he’d take the money and run like a thief.

grounded_facts: Galvin responds sarcastically to the judge's advice, rejecting both the suggestion and the implied authority.
memories.memory_text: I responded to the judge with sarcasm because I wasn't going to accept his condescending advice.

grounded_facts: A private meeting in Judge Sweeney's chambers involving Galvin, Concannon, and the judge, discussing settlement before trial.
memories.memory_text: I was in Judge Sweeney's chambers with Concannon and the judge, sitting in silence after a tense discussion about settling the case before trial.

grounded_facts: Galvin walks to the jury box and begins questioning prospective juror Abrams, showing signs of nervousness.
memories.memory_text: I walked over to the jury box to question Mr. Abrams, and I remember feeling very nervous as I did it.

grounded_facts: A formal process in the courtroom where attorneys question prospective jurors to determine suitability for service.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that this was the formal jury selection process where attorneys question prospective jurors to assess their suitability, though I wasn't certain how smoothly it would go with Abrams.

grounded_facts: Galvin begins questioning Mr. Abrams about his hospital experience as part of jury selection.
Galvin asks Mr. Abrams whether he has been treated in a hospital and how he was treated, as part of jury vetting.
memories.memory_text: I approached Mr. Abrams in the jury box and began asking him about his hospital experience, including whether he had been treated in a hospital and how that treatment went, as part of the jury selection process.

grounded_facts: Mickey reports that Mary Rooney, the obstetric nurse, refused to speak with him at the hospital and that he plans to approach her at home.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mickey reports that Mary Rooney, the obstetric nurse, refused to speak with him at the hospital and that he plans to approach her at home.

grounded_facts: Galvin reads a newspaper article and learns that Dr. Towler, his expert witness, is receiving public honors and media attention, which Mickey implies may indicate bias or external support for the defense.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Galvin reads a newspaper article and learns that Dr. Towler, his expert witness, is receiving public honors and media attention, which Mickey implies may indicate bias or external support for the defense.

grounded_facts: Mickey hands Galvin a newspaper and points out Dr. Towler's public honors and upcoming TV appearance to suggest institutional bias.
memories.memory_text: I remember that Mickey hands Galvin a newspaper and points out Dr. Towler's public honors and upcoming TV appearance to suggest institutional bias.

grounded_facts: Galvin, realizing he must see Gruber, asks Mickey to meet Laura Fischer at O'Rourke's on his behalf and relay that he will come later.
Galvin asks Mickey to inform Laura Fischer that he cannot meet her at O'Rourke's but will come later.
memories.memory_text: I realized I had to go see Gruber, so I asked Mickey to meet Laura Fischer at O'Rourke's and tell her I couldn't make it on time but would come by later.

grounded_facts: An informal encounter between Mickey and Galvin in the courthouse corridor, involving updates on the case and personal errands.
memories.memory_text: I remember that An informal encounter between Mickey and Galvin in the courthouse corridor, involving updates on the case and personal errands.

grounded_facts: Galvin dismisses Mickey's concern about the defense's media advantage, insisting he will try the case his own way and win.
Despite pressure from Mickey and the revelation of the defense's public support, Galvin asserts his intention to pursue the case independently and confidently claims he will win.
memories.memory_text: I told Mickey not to worry about me, and when he showed me the article about the defense getting public support, I said 'So what?'—because I’m going to try this case my way and I’m going to win it, even if Concannon has the media on his side.

grounded_facts: Galvin tells Doneghy he would accept the settlement now if he could, but reveals it has been withdrawn by the other side.
In response to Doneghy's anger, Galvin reveals that he would have accepted the $200,000 settlement if possible, but the offer has since been retracted.
memories.memory_text: I told Doneghy that if I could accept the $200,000 settlement right now, I would—but I also told him they took it back.

grounded_facts: Doneghy physically confronts Galvin, accusing him of destroying his life by rejecting the settlement without consent and threatening disbarment.
Doneghy confronts Galvin angrily, accusing him of ruining his life by rejecting a $200,000 settlement offer without consultation, and threatens disbarment.
memories.memory_text: I remember Doneghy confronting me in the courthouse lobby, getting in my face and accusing me of ruining his life by rejecting the $200,000 settlement without talking to him first—he said he was going to have me disbarred and made it clear he felt betrayed.

grounded_facts: A hostile, unscheduled encounter in the courthouse lobby where Doneghy confronts Galvin over the rejected settlement and its personal consequences.
memories.memory_text: I remember that A hostile, unscheduled encounter in the courthouse lobby where Doneghy confronts Galvin over the rejected settlement and its personal consequences.

grounded_facts: Mickey asks Laura for a cigarette, marking the first personal request in their interaction.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mickey asked Laura for a cigarette, making it the first personal request in their interaction.

grounded_facts: Mickey Morrissey approaches Laura at the bar and introduces himself as someone who is supposed to get to know her, replacing Franky who couldn't make it.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Mickey Morrissey approached Laura at the bar and introduced himself as the one supposed to get to know her because I couldn't make it.

grounded_facts: A planned personal meeting at a pub where Laura waits for Franky, who sends Mickey instead to connect with her.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that there had been a planned meeting at the pub where Laura waited for me, but I sent Mickey instead to connect with her.

grounded_facts: Galvin arrives at a restricted hospital area and brings out a box of Macanudo Cigars, indicating an intention to use them in a social or strategic interaction.
memories.memory_text: I walked up to the 'Doctors Only' door, opened my briefcase, and took out the box of Macanudo Cigars, smiling to myself as I prepared to go inside.

grounded_facts: A scheduled appointment between Galvin and Dr. Gruber set for 7:00 P.M. at the hospital.
memories.memory_text: I think my appointment with Dr. Gruber is set for 7:00 P.M. at the hospital, based on what I saw in my book.

grounded_facts: Galvin confirms the time and location of his scheduled meeting with Dr. Gruber by consulting his appointment book.
memories.memory_text: I checked my appointment book to confirm the time and location of my meeting with Dr. Gruber.

grounded_facts: Galvin approaches the nurse and asks for Dr. Gruber, seeking his location or availability.
memories.memory_text: I approached the nurse and asked for Dr. Gruber, wanting to know if he was available.

grounded_facts: Galvin discovers that Dr. Gruber is not at the hospital and has not been seen all day, raising concern.
memories.memory_text: I learned from the nurse that Dr. Gruber wasn't at the hospital and hadn't been seen all day, which made me concerned.

grounded_facts: Galvin reaches the brownstone building where Dr. Gruber's office is located, indicating an intention to meet or seek help.
memories.memory_text: I walked through the snow to Dr. Gruber's brownstone, looking to meet him at his office, and I saw the dark, empty interior through the window.

grounded_facts: Galvin attempts to gain entry to Gruber's office by knocking twice but receives no response, leading to disbelief.
memories.memory_text: I knocked on the door twice, but no one answered, and I stood there feeling unbelieving.

grounded_facts: Galvin urgently asks the maid to let him contact Dr. Gruber, claiming his wife needs a prescription refill, but is denied access.
memories.memory_text: I pleaded with the maid, telling her my wife's prescription had run out and I needed to call Dr. Gruber, but she refused to let me contact him, and I became desperate trying to explain I had to talk to him.

grounded_facts: Galvin arrives at Dr. Gruber's house, knocks repeatedly, but receives no answer; the maid later confirms Dr. Gruber is not available and is unreachable on a Caribbean island.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at Dr. Gruber's house, knocked repeatedly, and got no answer; I felt defeated as I started down the stairs, only to hear the door open behind me and the maid tell me he wasn't in and would be gone for a week, unreachable.

grounded_facts: Galvin asks Judge Sweeney for an extension in his case due to a missing witness.
memories.memory_text: I asked Judge Sweeney for an extension because my witness disappeared, and I told him I could subpoena the witness if I had a week.

grounded_facts: Judge Sweeney refuses to grant Galvin an extension and criticizes his decision to go to trial unprepared.
memories.memory_text: Judge Sweeney told me I should have taken their offer and criticized me for going to trial unprepared, saying this case never should have come to trial.

grounded_facts: An informal, after-hours encounter between Galvin and Judge Sweeney in the Judge's home study.
memories.memory_text: I went to Judge Sweeney's study after hours, knocked on the door, and went inside to talk to him about my case.

grounded_facts: The Judge turns up the TV volume, signaling dismissal after refusing Galvin's request.
memories.memory_text: I saw the Judge lean forward and turn up the TV volume, which made it clear he was dismissing me after refusing my request.

grounded_facts: Galvin repeatedly asks the operator to help him contact Mr. Alito, despite being told it's outside business hours and against policy.
Galvin attempts to reach Mr. Alito outside business hours, requesting his home number or a callback due to an urgent matter.
memories.memory_text: I was shivering at a street corner phone, trying to reach Mr. Alito because I knew the situation was urgent, and I asked the operator to help me get his home number or have him call me back, even though she said it was against policy outside business hours.

grounded_facts: Galvin informs the opposing firm that his client wishes to accept their $200,000 settlement offer, despite his own objections.
memories.memory_text: I called the opposing firm to tell them my client wanted to accept their $200,000 settlement offer, even though I tried to talk her out of it—I was shocked by her decision and felt like she'd come down with nerves at the last minute.

grounded_facts: Mickey enters the office and repeatedly asks Galvin what happened, showing visible worry.
memories.memory_text: I remember Mickey coming into the office and asking me what happened, then calling me 'Joey' and asking again, but I didn't answer when he asked if I met with Dr. Gruber.

grounded_facts: Galvin realizes that Concannon has already contacted Dr. Thompson, his potential witness, undermining his case.
memories.memory_text: I realized Concannon had already gotten to Dr. Thompson, my potential witness, which undermined my case.

grounded_facts: Mickey picks up Galvin's cigars but throws them across the room in disgust, symbolizing his disapproval of Galvin's current state or choices.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mickey pick up my Macanudo cigars from the desk and then throw them across the room in disgust, clearly upset with me and the way I've been handling things.

grounded_facts: Galvin informs Laura that the opposition has reached his witness, indicating a serious development in the case.
memories.memory_text: I told Laura that they got to my witness, and I could feel everything unraveling because of it.

grounded_facts: Laura reassures Galvin, encourages him to rest, and offers to stay with him, providing emotional stability during his distress.
memories.memory_text: Laura told me I couldn't work if I couldn't think, urged me to rest, and said she’d stay with me, which made me ask if she really would—and I finally agreed I’d only rest a little while.

grounded_facts: An informal, emotionally charged interaction between Galvin and Laura in Galvin's apartment at night, triggered by a setback in his case.
memories.memory_text: I was in my apartment at night, feeling distraught and frightened after a serious reversal in my case when Laura came in; I told her we had a setback, that they got to my witness, and I kept insisting I had to work, even as she reassured me, told me to rest, and offered to stay with me—so I asked if she really would, and said I'd only rest a little while.

grounded_facts: Galvin, after being urged by Laura, agrees to rest briefly in bed, marking a shift from active work to temporary withdrawal due to stress.
memories.memory_text: I told Laura I was only going to rest a little while, and she led me into the bedroom, helping me step away from everything for now.

grounded_facts: Galvin recognizes and greets Dr. Thompson upon his arrival at South Street Station, initiating their meeting.
memories.memory_text: I recognized Dr. Thompson as he approached, and I greeted him by saying, 'Dr. Thompson...?' before we shook hands.

grounded_facts: Galvin acknowledges Dr. Thompson, cuts off his thanks, takes his bag, and expresses gratitude for his arrival, establishing a respectful and welcoming tone.
memories.memory_text: When Dr. Thompson started to thank me for meeting him, I cut him off and said, 'Thank you for coming,' then I took his bag and we shook hands, making sure he felt welcome.

grounded_facts: A meeting arranged at South Street Station in Boston to greet Dr. Thompson upon his arrival by train.
memories.memory_text: I was waiting at South Street Station in Boston, watching the arriving passengers, because I had arranged to meet Dr. Thompson when he got off the train.

grounded_facts: Galvin disposes of his boutonniere upon entering the station, symbolizing a shift from formality or personal sentiment to a more pragmatic mindset.
memories.memory_text: I dropped my boutonniere in the wastebasket as I walked in, leaving behind the formality it represented and focusing myself on the work ahead.

grounded_facts: Galvin decides to take Dr. Thompson to see the girl at his home, marking a key step in involving him in the case.
memories.memory_text: I decided to take Dr. Thompson to the home to see the girl, so he could finally meet her and get involved in the case.

grounded_facts: A planned occasion where Galvin will bring Dr. Thompson to his home to meet the girl involved in the case.
memories.memory_text: I told Dr. Thompson I'm going to take him to the home to meet the girl, so he can see for himself what this case is really about.

grounded_facts: Galvin strongly urges Dr. Thompson to stay at his apartment instead of a hotel, citing potential danger from the opposition.
Galvin expresses concern about the powerful and aggressive forces opposing the case, urging Dr. Thompson to stay at his apartment for safety.
memories.memory_text: I urged Dr. Thompson to stay at my apartment instead of a hotel because I know how rough these people can be — they don't want to lose this case, and I was worried they might come after him.

grounded_facts: Dr. Thompson responds to Galvin's warning by asserting that the opposition cannot affect him.
memories.memory_text: I warned Dr. Thompson about the pressure the opposition could bring, but he smiled and told me there was nothing they could do to him.

grounded_facts: Galvin persuades Dr. Thompson to stay at his place for the evening and provides him with an envelope containing the address and key.
memories.memory_text: I persuaded Dr. Thompson to stay at my place for the evening, handed him an envelope with my address and the key, and emphasized the need for discretion.

grounded_facts: Galvin asks Dr. Thompson not to tell anyone about his presence at the location.
memories.memory_text: I instructed Dr. Thompson not to tell anyone about his presence at my place, asking him to keep his stay completely confidential.

grounded_facts: Galvin learns from Mickey that the obstetric nurse is at home and decides to go see her immediately.
memories.memory_text: I learned from Mickey that the obstetric nurse was at home, so I decided to go see her right away.

grounded_facts: Galvin interrupts Mickey's plan to talk to the nurse and asserts his intention to go himself.
memories.memory_text: I interrupted Mickey when he was about to talk to the nurse and told him I'd handle it myself because I need her for the case.

grounded_facts: A face-to-face encounter at Mary Rooney's home where Joe Galvin attempts to extract information about a medical malpractice case.
memories.memory_text: I remember showing up at Mary Rooney's home, introducing myself as Joe Galvin representing Deborah Ann Kaye, and confronting her face-to-face about the malpractice case, trying to get her to talk.

grounded_facts: Galvin warns Mary that he can subpoena her to testify in court if she refuses to speak now.
Galvin threatens to legally compel Mary Rooney's testimony in court if she continues to refuse to speak with him voluntarily.
memories.memory_text: I told Mary I can subpoena her if she won't talk, because I need her to testify about what happened in that operating room.

grounded_facts: Galvin repeatedly questions Mary about what happened in the operating room, insisting she knows the truth and implying she is protecting the doctors.
memories.memory_text: I kept pressing Mary, asking her what went wrong in the O.R., convinced she knows why Towler and Marx caused the injury, and I directly challenged her about who she's protecting.

grounded_facts: Galvin visits Mary Rooney to pressure her into revealing information about a medical incident in the operating room involving Deborah Ann Kaye, implying she knows the truth but is protecting someone.
memories.memory_text: I went to Mary Rooney's house to pressure her into revealing what happened in the operating room during Deborah Ann Kaye's procedure, making it clear I believe she knows the truth but is protecting the doctors.

grounded_facts: After repeated pressure, Mary Rooney refuses to testify and delivers a scathing condemnation of lawyers, accusing them of lacking loyalty and caring only about money.
memories.memory_text: I tried to get Mary Rooney to testify, even reminding her I could subpoena her, but she refused and lashed out at me, saying lawyers are all whores who don't care who gets hurt and only care about money.

grounded_facts: Mary accuses Galvin and lawyers in general of being unethical, disloyal, and motivated solely by money.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mary accuse me and all lawyers of being unethical, disloyal, and motivated only by money when I pressed her to cooperate.

grounded_facts: Mickey briefly breaks off questioning to look at Galvin and shrug, signaling uncertainty or concern about the direction of the interrogation.
After aggressive questioning, Mickey briefly drops his belligerent tone and consults Galvin non-verbally, indicating a tactical shift in the cross-examination approach.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mickey break off the questioning and turn to me, dropping his aggressive tone, and he gave me a slight shrug like he was unsure what to do next—I nodded to let him know we should keep going.

grounded_facts: Galvin enters the hotel room and immediately declares that they are going to lose the case, expressing self-doubt and resignation.
memories.memory_text: I walked into the hotel room, closed the door, hung up my coat, and told Laura we're going to lose — I said it's over, and I never should have taken the case.

grounded_facts: A private, emotionally charged encounter between Galvin and Laura in her hotel room, where professional failure and personal immaturity are confronted.
memories.memory_text: I confronted Laura in her hotel room, feeling broken and unsure, asking if it's my fault we're going to lose, and when she called me like a kid avoiding school, I felt exposed and asked what it was to her — only to hear she can't invest in failure.

grounded_facts: Overwhelmed by emotional pressure, Galvin abruptly leaves the room and locks himself in the bathroom, struggling to breathe.
memories.memory_text: I got up suddenly and rushed out of the room, locking myself in the bathroom because I couldn't catch my breath and my chest was heaving—I just couldn't handle the pressure anymore.

grounded_facts: While having a panic attack, Galvin screams at Laura to stop pressuring him, deflecting her concern as external blame.
memories.memory_text: I screamed at Laura to stop pressuring me while I was having a panic attack, even though she was just trying to help.

grounded_facts: Laura counters Galvin's accusation by stating that he is pressuring himself, urging acceptance and release.
Laura knocks on the bathroom door and enters despite resistance, asserting that Galvin is pressuring himself and must let go.
memories.memory_text: I remember Laura knocking and then coming into the bathroom, telling me that I was pressuring myself and saying we all have to let go.

grounded_facts: Laura refuses to comfort Galvin, instead accusing him of childish behavior and blaming himself prematurely.
memories.memory_text: I asked Laura if she thought it was my fault, and I could feel myself falling apart, but she didn't comfort me—instead she told me I was acting like a child, avoiding responsibility, and that it was probably my fault, and I just kept saying it was over.

grounded_facts: Galvin tells Sally he will do his best and emphasizes how personally meaningful the case is to him.
memories.memory_text: I told Sally I would do my best for her and her sister, and I meant it — I made sure she knew how much this case means to me personally.

grounded_facts: Mickey refers to their expert witness as a 'witch doctor,' indicating low confidence in their medical testimony.
memories.memory_text: I heard Mickey say we've got nothing but a 'witch doctor' for our expert, which made me realize how little he thinks of our case.

grounded_facts: Mickey jokes that it's 'refreshing' when a doctor on the stand isn't Jewish, revealing prejudiced views.
memories.memory_text: Mickey told me it was 'refreshing' when a doctor on the stand isn't Jewish, and I knew then he was revealing his own prejudice.

grounded_facts: Galvin confirms to the judge that the plaintiff is ready to proceed with the trial.
memories.memory_text: I confirmed to the judge that I was ready to proceed with the trial on behalf of the plaintiff.

grounded_facts: Concannon confirms to the judge that the defense is ready to proceed with the trial.
memories.memory_text: I saw Concannon confirm that the defense was ready to proceed after I did.

grounded_facts: The formal opening of the trial in the Superior Court, where both parties declare readiness and the plaintiff delivers an opening statement.
memories.memory_text: I stood before the jury in the Superior Court and delivered my opening statement, knowing I had to balance justice, mercy, and impartiality while honoring the gravity of what Deborah Ann Kaye has suffered.

grounded_facts: Galvin begins his opening statement to the jury, framing the case as a moral and legal judgment on medical negligence that destroyed his client's life.
memories.memory_text: I began my opening statement to the jury, framing the case as a moral and legal judgment on the medical negligence that destroyed my client's life.

grounded_facts: The court formally admits Dr. Thompson as an expert witness after Concannon's sarcastic concession.
memories.memory_text: I remember when Concannon finally gave in with sarcasm, saying they’d admit Dr. Thompson as an 'expert witness,' and the court accepted it.

grounded_facts: Concannon aggressively questions Dr. Thompson about his lack of board certifications and paid expert testimony to undermine his authority.
memories.memory_text: I saw Concannon press Dr. Thompson hard, questioning whether he was board-certified and pointing out he's been paid to testify before, clearly trying to undermine his credibility.

grounded_facts: The judge sustains an objection and limits Dr. Thompson's testimony to the review of hospital records, disallowing personal examination findings.
memories.memory_text: I was in the courtroom when the judge sustained the objection and told Dr. Thompson to limit his testimony to the hospital records, which blocked me from using his personal findings.

grounded_facts: Dr. Thompson testifies that the cardiac arrest resuscitation took nine to ten minutes, contradicting Dr. Towler's claim of three to four minutes, citing extensive brain damage as evidence.
memories.memory_text: I heard Dr. Thompson testify that the resuscitation took nine to ten minutes because of the extent of brain damage, which contradicted Dr. Towler's claim of three to four minutes.

grounded_facts: The judge interrupts and rephrases the standard of negligence narrowly, forcing Dr. Thompson to concede that a nine-minute delay alone does not constitute negligence.
memories.memory_text: I was trying to question my witness my own way when the judge interrupted and rephrased the standard of negligence, forcing Dr. Thompson to admit that a nine-minute delay alone wouldn't count as negligence.

grounded_facts: Ongoing trial in which Dr. Thompson testifies as an expert witness regarding the medical events surrounding Deborah Ann Kaye's condition.
memories.memory_text: I was in the middle of examining Dr. Thompson about the medical events in Deborah Ann Kaye's case when the judge interrupted me.

grounded_facts: Galvin openly challenges the judge's interference, accusing him of trying and losing the case on his behalf.
Galvin objects to the judge's interference in his examination and asserts his right to conduct the questioning.
memories.memory_text: I stood up to the judge because I felt he was trying to take over my case and undermine my questioning—I told him I wasn't through with the witness and that if he was going to try the case for me, I'd rather he didn't lose it.

grounded_facts: The judge ends the morning session and summons Galvin to his chambers, signaling a serious reprimand or procedural consequence.
memories.memory_text: I remember the judge abruptly ending the morning session and summoning me to his chambers, which felt like a direct response to my challenge and signaled that I was about to face serious consequences.

grounded_facts: Galvin directly attacks the judge's professional integrity, accusing him of being a corrupt 'Bag Man' unfit for the bench.
memories.memory_text: I told the judge I knew who he really was — that he couldn't hack it as a lawyer and was just a Bag Man for the Boys, and that he's still corrupt and unfit for the bench.

grounded_facts: Galvin declares his intention to request a mistrial and the judge's disqualification, threatening to escalate to the state for impeachment.
memories.memory_text: I told Judge Sweeney I was done with his bias, that I'd be asking for a mistrial and demanding he disqualify himself, and that I'd take the transcript to the State to have his ass impeached.

grounded_facts: A heated private confrontation between Galvin and Judge Sweeney in the judge's chambers following official reprimand.
memories.memory_text: I was furious when Judge Sweeney confronted me in his chambers, threatening to have me removed, but I stood my ground — I told him all I wanted was an even shake, that he rushed me into trial and denied me fairness, that I knew he was a corrupt 'Bag Man' who couldn't hack it as a lawyer, and that I'd be asking for a mistrial, his disqualification, and impeachment if necessary.

grounded_facts: Judge Sweeney threatens to have Galvin arrested and jailed if he does not leave the chambers immediately.
memories.memory_text: I remember Judge Sweeney threatening to have me arrested and thrown in jail if I didn't leave his chambers immediately after my outburst.

grounded_facts: Galvin reassures Sally that he will have the same chance to present his side and cross-examine after the defense presents their case.
memories.memory_text: I reassured Sally that after the defense presents their case, I’ll have the same chance to present our side and cross-examine.

grounded_facts: Sally asks Galvin about the meaning of the proceedings and whether they are going to win, showing desperation for trust in their strategy.
memories.memory_text: Sally asked me if we were going to win, and I could hear the worry in her voice as she looked to me for answers.

grounded_facts: The spectators are reentering the courtroom for the afternoon session, indicating the continuation of the trial.
memories.memory_text: I noticed the spectators reentering the courtroom for the afternoon session, so I knew the trial was continuing.

grounded_facts: After parting with Sally, Galvin notices Mickey by the courtroom door; they lock eyes and share a moment of silent acknowledgment.
memories.memory_text: After I said goodbye to Sally, I turned toward the courtroom and saw Mickey standing by the door; we locked eyes and shared a quiet moment of understanding without saying a word.

grounded_facts: Dr. Towler is on the witness stand being cross-examined by Galvin about the medical events during Deborah Ann Kaye's surgery and resuscitation.
memories.memory_text: I saw Dr. Towler on the witness stand, and I got up from my table to begin cross-examining him about Deborah Ann Kaye's surgery and resuscitation.

grounded_facts: Galvin questions Dr. Towler about the gap in medical notations after the patient's heart stopped, attempting to establish negligence.
memories.memory_text: I questioned Dr. Towler about the gap in the medical notations after Deborah Ann Kaye's heart stopped, trying to show negligence by pointing out what wasn't recorded during those missing minutes.

grounded_facts: Dr. Towler counters Galvin's line of questioning by explaining that the patient's anemia meant her brain was already receiving less oxygen, so brain damage could have occurred in as little as two minutes.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Dr. Towler that the patient was anemic and her brain was already getting less oxygen, so brain damage could have happened in just a few minutes.

grounded_facts: Galvin realizes he has made a critical mistake during the cross-examination of Dr. Towler when the doctor reveals that the patient's anemia could have caused brain damage much earlier, undermining Galvin's argument about the nine-minute gap.
memories.memory_text: I realized I had made a critical mistake when Dr. Towler revealed the anemia, and I looked to Mickey for support, seeing him shake his head sadly.

grounded_facts: Dr. Thompson admits he believes he did not perform well in court, seeking reassurance or validation from Galvin.
memories.memory_text: I heard Dr. Thompson tell me he didn't do too well for me, and I could sense his doubt.

grounded_facts: Galvin attempts to comfort Dr. Thompson by saying he did fine, despite Thompson's doubts.
memories.memory_text: I told Dr. Thompson he did fine, even though he seemed unsure about how he performed in court.

grounded_facts: Dr. Thompson makes an observation about people's capacity to hear the truth, possibly offering encouragement or commentary on the trial.
memories.memory_text: I recall Dr. Thompson saying that people sometimes have a great capacity to hear the truth, as if trying to find hope in how the trial was going.

grounded_facts: Dr. Thompson offers to remain available for the case until Monday, showing continued concern and commitment despite his perceived poor performance.
memories.memory_text: I remember Dr. Thompson offering to stay on until Monday, asking me twice if I wanted him to remain available.

grounded_facts: Galvin declines Dr. Thompson's offer and tells him to go home, ending his involvement for the day.
memories.memory_text: I told Dr. Thompson no, thanked him, and told him to go home so he could rest after his testimony.

grounded_facts: Mickey exits the courtroom and announces he is returning to the office, indicating continued work outside the courtroom.
memories.memory_text: I saw Mickey leave the courtroom and heard him say, 'I'm going back to the office,' so I knew he was continuing to work while I stayed behind.

grounded_facts: An informal gathering in the courthouse corridor immediately after Dr. Thompson's testimony, involving Galvin and Dr. Thompson.

memories.memory_text: I handed my card to Mrs. Dee like it was something she needed to take, the way you'd press a bill into someone's hand so they wouldn't refuse it — I could feel the ten-dollar bribe still warm in my pocket from the funeral director.
I reached into my pocket for my card, trying to speak to the widow, and the son stepped in front of her, demanding what that was—my card—his voice sharp, confused, then angry.
He slapped the card from my hand, shouted that I didn’t know his father, and told me to get out—then the funeral manager grabbed me, pushed me toward the back while the son kept yelling behind me.
I was just trying to talk to someone inside, and the manager told me not to come back, then shoved me—right in front of everyone. I stood there watching people go in, not knowing where to go next.
I threw my law degrees into the wastebasket, one after the other, and stared at the empty wall where they used to hang — it didn't make a bit of difference anymore.
I walked down that dim corridor, file in hand, matching door numbers, feeling the attendants' eyes on me like I didn't belong—then found her room and went in.
I opened the door to the dark ward, unsteady on my feet, and set down my file and briefcase before pulling out the cheap Polaroid from my bag—I needed pictures of her, proof of what they’d done.
After taking the photos, I sat on the end of her bed, lit a cigarette, and just looked at her—there was no sound, just the tubes and the stillness, and something in me quieted.

I saw her at Northern Care—lying there, unresponsive, the woman Sally and Dick love like a daughter. I could see the weight of it in Sally’s voice, how helpless they both felt, and when she asked if I’d seen her, I had to say yes. It wasn’t just a case anymore.

Sally said this was their chance to get away, her voice breaking—Dick called about the job in Tucson, the Archdiocese poking around—and I told them, 'I’m going to see you get that chance.' I meant it. Not just the settlement, but their escape. I couldn’t let that slip.

I was juggling these heavy textbooks, trying to get my key out while still reading—couldn't put the book down, not even for a second—because I needed to understand anesthesiology, really understand it, if I was going to make any sense of this case.

I remember the moment Claire told me Dr. Gruber wanted to meet about testifying—'he wants to testify...?'—and I could feel the case shifting, like the ground finally giving under my feet after all the running in place.

The phone rang, Claire said it was the Bishop's office, and when she asked if I wanted to take it, I waved her off—'I'm not in'—but then agreed to a meeting tomorrow at two, knowing full well that call meant they were ready to settle.

Gruber looked at me and said, 'Her doctors murdered her,' like it was that simple — I remember the weight of those words hitting me, standing there on the stairs, the way he repeated it to make sure I couldn't look away.

I took a cigar from Gruber, not really thinking, and tried to light it — my hand was shaking, I didn’t even notice I hadn’t bitten the end off, and when I finally got it lit, it felt like I was holding onto something just to keep my hands from showing how much that conversation got to me.

I asked Gruber why he was doing this, standing there in the cold parking lot, my cigar half-lit, and he just said, 'To do right. Isn't that why you're doing it?' — like he was looking straight through me.

I was on the phone, trying to steady someone who was falling apart, telling them to move on, to go west, that they had their own life — all while my eyes kept drifting to the Polaroids of Deborah Ann on the legal pad, and those crossed-out numbers: $250,000, $225,000 circled too many times.

After I hung up, I reached for the bottle and saw her — the blonde in the silver frame, laughing on a sailboat — and next to it, my ring buried in a pile of change, the rosary there too; I just sat in the dark afterward, head back, not moving.
I looked at the settlement number—$210,000—and it hit me how cleanly it divided by three. I’d get seventy thousand. That wasn’t just compensation; it was a cut, a silent share in the cover-up.
I pushed the paper away and said I couldn’t take the money—because if I did, I’d be lost, just a rich ambulance chaser, paid to look the other way like everyone else.

I walked into the lawyers' room, saw Mickey playing cards, and knew I couldn't wait anymore—I had to get him out of there. I pulled him up and said, 'Come on. Let's get a drink,' then led him into the corridor.
I told Mickey I turned down the two hundred ten grand because they killed her and are trying to buy it — I can't let that stand. I have to stand up for her, even if he thinks I'm crazy.
I reminded Mickey of his own words — 'if not now, when' — and asked him to help me, because I can't do this alone. I needed him to see this wasn't just about winning, but about doing something real.
I remember saying that the court isn't there to give the weak justice, but just a chance at it—like that idea kept me going, sitting there with Laura, smoke in the air, the hum of the bar behind us.
I can still feel the pause before I said, 'Maybe I can do something right,' and then her asking if that's what I'd do—like she was testing me—and I told her that's what I was going to try to do.
I walked into the judge’s chambers late, saw him eating bacon and eggs with Concannon like they were sharing breakfast at a club, and muttered an apology when he called me out for being late.
When the judge tried to push a quick settlement, I cut him off—this wasn’t about deal-making, and I wasn’t there to play along like everything was arranged.
I walked up to the 'Doctors Only' door, opened my briefcase, and took out the box of Macanudo Cigars—felt the weight of it in my hand—then stepped inside, smiling just a little.

I stood at that door, pounding it like a fool, and when the maid finally answered, she told me Gruber was unreachable—on some island in the Caribbean with no phone, coming back in a week. I still had the cigars in my hand, useless now, just like me.

I stood at that phone booth in the snow, shivering, trying to get through to Alito—my fingers numb, the wind cutting through my coat, but I kept pressing the receiver hard against my ear, insisting it was an emergency, that he had to call me back in half an hour.
I told Sally I’d do my best for her and her sister, and I meant it—more than she could know. It means that much to me.

I stood before the jury, took a breath, and began—telling them how heavy judgment is, how they’ve likely prayed for guidance. I named the two doctors and the hospital, then laid out what we’d prove: Deborah Ann Kaye was robbed of everything by their negligence.

I told Sweeney I just wanted an even shake — rushed into court in five days, my witness gone, no continuance — but I didn’t back down. I said the hell with it, I’m trying this case and letting the jury decide, even if he’s known as a defendant’s judge.

I called him out — told him not to feed me that 'I was a lawyer too' line, that he was a Bag Man then and still is. When he asked if I was done, I said damn right, and told him I’d ask for a mistrial, his disqualification, and have his ass impeached.

I was pressing Dr. Towler on the three-minute gap in the notations after Deborah Kaye's heart stopped, trying to show they weren't doing enough, when he hit me with the anemia explanation—and I realized I’d walked right into it. I’d lost control of the moment, and Mickey’s look told me everything.
I kept pacing, not stopping, not answering, because I couldn't let it end like this — when Mickey said the case was over, I turned on him, sharp, like a cornered animal, and made him choose.

We have been paid to look the other way. I came in here to take your money. (beat) I brought snapshots to show you. So I could get your money.

They might. Yes. That's the point... is that they might... you see, the jury wants to believe. They're all cynics, sure, because they want to believe. I have to go in there tomorrow to find twelve people to hear this case. I'm going to see a hundred people and pick twelve. And every one of them it's written on their face, 'This is a sham. There is no justice...' but in their heart they're saying, 'Maybe... maybe...'
And don't give me this shit, 'I was a lawyer, too.' 'Cause I know who you were. You couldn't hack it as a lawyer. You were Bag Man for the Boys and you still are. I know who you are.
I'm an attorney on trial before the bar. Representing my client. My client, do you understand? You open your mouth and you're losing my case for me.

It's a terrible thing to sit in judgment. So much rides on it. I know that you've thought, 'How can I be pure. How can I be impartial without being cold. How can I be merciful and still be just?' And I know that most of you have said some sort of prayer this morning to be helped. To judge correctly. We have the reputation of two men. Two well respected doctors and a renowned hospital before us. And with those two respected men we have my client, Deborah Ann Kaye...
I'm not through with the witness, your Honor. With all due respect if you are going to try my case for me I would appreciate it if you wouldn't lose it.

I told him my ex-husband was a lawyer, and he didn’t flinch—just said it was wonderful, like he was testing me. I remember how I held back, not saying who ended it, not letting him think he knew me that easy.
He said I came back to see him, and I tried to push back—what if it wasn’t you? But then he just stood up and asked if I’d eaten, like he already knew I’d follow. And I did.
I asked him if they were going to get justice, watching his face in the dim light, the smoke between us curling like doubt.
I leaned in a little, voice low, and asked again—'Is that what you're going to do?'—needing to hear him say it out loud, not just think it.
I said it was all right to leave the picture out, then I started taking off my blouse—my hands were slow, I remember the fabric at my shoulders, and how he just stood there watching.
I asked Mickey how I was doing, and when he said I was great, I offered him a cigarette and asked what he was drinking—then called the bartender by name, like I belonged there.

I remember sitting at the bar, the weight of Mickey's story about Frank pressing on me—how he started out idealistic, then broken by the system, just like so many others. When Mickey asked if I liked the story, I just looked at him, unable to speak, the truth of it too heavy to answer.
I asked if he wanted me to leave, and when he said no, I told him to get in bed — that I’d stay with him. Then I led him into the bedroom.
Later, I was sitting in his robe, reading a book, smoking — just watching the bedroom door. I remember putting the book down and taking a slow drag, waiting.
I told him he was talking like a drunk, and when he said it was over, I asked him what he was doing here—if he wanted to leave or even kill himself. I couldn’t let him collapse like that.

He shut himself in the bathroom, couldn’t breathe, and when he screamed at me to stop pressuring him, I opened the door and said, 'You're pressuring yourself.' I had to make him see it wasn’t all on me.
I stepped out into the corridor after the trial, looked around carefully, and walked over to him—just stood there near Galvin, not saying anything at first.
I asked him if it was over, and then what he was going to do—my voice felt tight, like the words might not come out right, but I needed to know.
He handed me the red-backed document—Confidential, Eyes only—without a smile, just 'Welcome back,' and I took it, feeling the weight of it in my hands.

I picked up the envelope from the floor, opened it by the dim light from the window, and read his handwriting—'I'm going to try. When this is over can we go away?' I just sat there, holding the paper, not moving.

I walked in with the coffee, handed him his, and said I needed to talk—just those words, 'I have to talk to you'—but he didn't stop, didn't really look, just said he couldn't now and went back to the phone, already dialing another number.
I was standing by the wall phone, so tired, when the owner handed me the tray with the coffees and cigarettes—I took the change and turned toward the phone, not sure yet who to call.
I must have fallen asleep on the couch in Galvin's office, and when I woke up, I could feel his overcoat over me—he must have put it there.
I was half-awake, cold, wrapped in Galvin's coat on the couch, and I could feel him standing over me, looking down, before he moved away.

I woke up to the phone ringing, and when Joe said he was going to New York, I felt a jolt—like something shifted. I told him I was going too, for the divorce papers, and asked if we could meet at the Beacon, just after four.

After I hung up, Mickey asked for a cigarette. I didn’t see him go through my purse, didn’t know he’d seen the red-backed report on Joe—my notes, the notations. He stood there, quiet, after putting it back. I didn’t know he knew.
I sat there with my coffee, not drinking it, just watching the door—waiting, but not letting myself hope too much.

I saw him walk toward me, and I knew—he finally knew. I tried to say something, but the words wouldn’t come, and then he hit me, knocked me down, the table crashing over. I just kept saying it’s all right, over and over, like that could stop anything.
I stood in the corridor, just watching him—unsure if he saw me, unsure if I wanted him to.
I stood at the end of the corridor holding the yellow paper, my hand trembling, waiting for him to see it—waiting for any sign—but he turned away.

memories.memory_text: I walked in and saw Frank passed out on the couch again, bottle on the floor, phone off the hook — same damn mess, same damn man. I told him Sally Doneghy called, that he was supposed to be in court, and he didn’t even know who she was.

I knocked the drink out of his hand and slapped him — hard — because he kept treating this like a joke. I told him I was done, that life was too short and I was too old to keep cleaning up after him, then I walked out and slammed the door.
I told Claire to come back to work — someone had to keep that office running, and she was the only one who wouldn’t screw it up.
I called in a favor with Dr. Gruber’s office and told them to have him reach out — if Galvin had to drag his ass into this case, at least I’d hand him the witness on a plate.
Galvin barged in, dragged me up from my gin game, and said he needed to talk—like I wasn't in the middle of a hand. I told my partner not to touch anything before he pulled me out.
I yelled at Frank, asking if he was out of his mind for turning down two-hundred-ten grand — what was he going to do, bring the girl back to life?
He kept saying he had to stand up for that girl, and when he reminded me of my own words — 'if not now, when' — I didn't know what to say. He actually made me feel something.

I looked at the notes and told Frank the sister's testimony wouldn't work—jury would see right through it, no way to prove the hospital form wrong. But when he pushed Gruber, I admitted the guy wasn't bad.
I handed Galvin his cigar box and he asked me to tell Laura Fischer he’d meet her later — like I’m his damn messenger now.
Right after, Dick Doneghy came charging across the lobby, shoving Galvin into the wall — I moved to step in, but Galvin waved me off like it was nothing.
I walked up to Laura at the bar, told her Franky couldn't make it and I was stepping in—introduced myself, asked for a cigarette. She smiled, handed me one, and offered to buy me a drink.

Frank came to me in tears after finding out Stearns and Harrington bribed a juror on his case—he actually thought those people were saints because they knew what a 'spinnaker' was. I told him to wake up, those people are sharks, they didn’t get rich by doing good.

Frank came to me in tears after finding out Stearns and Harrington bribed a juror on his case. I told him they were sharks, not saints. Later, he called Harrington from jail and said he made a mistake. The charges were dropped, but he got fired, his wife left him, and he started drinking.

I walked in and saw Galvin on the phone, sweating, scrambling through files, trying to hold onto a case that was already gone—Concannon got to the witness, and he was just spinning, desperate to fix it.
I saw those Macanudo cigars on his desk—new, unopened—after all this time wasting my help, and I threw them across the room because it was all just bullshit.
I told Galvin the obstetric nurse was home after her late shift, and before I could finish, he demanded the address—said he was going over there himself.
I was pressing Thompson hard—why the wrong anesthetic, what a good doctor would do—trying to rattle him, make him slip up, but he wasn’t backing down easy.
I turned to check with Galvin, saw him nod, then shifted—asked casually about her care, but when I looked back at him and shrugged, I knew: this testimony isn’t saving us.
I looked at Galvin and said, 'How are you holding up?' then cracked that we've got a witch doctor—dark, but it had to be said, given what we're walking into.
I told Galvin I'm going back to the office and walked off, leaving him there alone in the corridor.
I told Frank the case was dead — no witness, our own expert says no negligence, what's left to fight? But he just kept pacing, not even hearing me, like he was chasing ghosts.
I was tired, just going through the motions, until Galvin asked who Mary Rooney was protecting—I snapped out of it and pushed back: 'All right. Who wasn't in the O.R.?'
When Galvin read out 'K.C.' and then 'Kathy Costello,' I latched onto it—something about the initials and the admitting nurse not being in the operating room clicked.

I pretended to be Dr. Dorchester, shouting into the phone that it was an emergency — a nurse had left my office four years ago and we needed a chart, but I kept having to stop because I needed a cigarette, my hands shaking from the stress.
I was asleep in the chair in Galvin's office when the mail came through the slot—I didn't even wake up until he moved around, and by then the weight of it all was already in the air.

I was digging through Laura's purse looking for a cigarette, and I found a pack—red-backed legal form underneath it, stamped 'CONFIDENTIAL. EYES ONLY!!!' from Concannon, Barker, White. That name hit me like a gut punch.

I pulled out that report—'Report on Joseph Galvin'—full of notes on his haunts and habits, scribbled in different pens. I just stood there, realizing she’d been digging into Joe behind my back. Then I put it back, closed the purse, and said nothing.
I saw Galvin coming down the street, all smiles, like nothing was wrong—so I stepped in, told him we had to talk, and started walking him away to talk somewhere private.
I told Joe about Laura working for one of Concannon's partners in New York, hoping he'd grasp how bad this was — she wanted to move to Boston, but that connection could blow the whole case apart.
I hung up the phone, went into the study, sat on the sofa, opened a bottle of whiskey, and poured a drink.
I poured a drink for him without a word, reached over, and offered it—just saw him sitting there in the dark, staring, but he shook his head no.
I saw Galvin sitting there like it was all over, head down, done — and then the foreman asked if they could award more than we asked for. That’s when I started to smile.
I turned my back on Laura right after Galvin did — didn’t say a word, just shut her out like he did. Felt heavy, but it was the only move that made sense after everything.
I offered Galvin a drink, kind of soft-like, not my usual tone — then he put his arm around my shoulder. We walked out together, just two guys leaning on each other without saying a word.
